entries.meaning: Rāma said that the sight of the sage’s feet had brought all their accumulated merit to fruition. He asked Vālmīki to name a place where they might stay without disturbing any sage or ascetic: those from whom ascetics suffer burn even without a king’s punitive fire; satisfying a brahmin is the root of blessing, while a holy person’s anger can consume millions of lineages. Knowing this, the sage should indicate a place where Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa could build an attractive shelter of leaves and grass and live for a while. Hearing Rāma’s naturally guileless words, the wise sage exclaimed, “Excellent!”—for how else could the banner of Raghu speak, when he always protects the bridge established by revelation?

Vālmīki replied: the world is there to be seen, but you are its seer, the one who makes Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva dance; even they do not know your mystery, so who else can know you? Only one to whom you reveal yourself knows you, and in knowing you becomes one with you. By your own grace devotees know you, Raghunandana, sandalwood cooling their hearts. Your body is made of consciousness and bliss, beyond change, as the qualified know; yet you have assumed a human body for saints and gods and speak and act like an ordinary king. The dull are bewildered and the wise delighted by hearing and seeing your deeds. Everything you say and do is true: an actor must dance in keeping with the costume assumed. You ask where you should live; I am embarrassed to ask in return—tell me where you are not, and then I shall show you a place.

Hearing the sage’s words steeped in the savor of love, Rāma smiled inwardly with modest reserve. Vālmīki laughed and continued in speech sweetly immersed in nectar: “Hear now, Rāma, the dwellings where you may live with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. Live in the lovely hearts of those whose ears are like oceans into which the many beautiful rivers of your stories continually pour without ever filling them. Those who have made their eyes into cātaka birds live longing for the raincloud of your vision; scorning rivers, seas, and great lakes, they are happy with a single drop of your beauty. Live with Sītā and your brother in the hearts of those devotees, giver of joy. And live in the heart of one whose swan-like tongue, moving upon the pure lake of your fame, selects the pearl-like multitude of your virtues.”

Live in the heart of one whose nose respectfully receives each day the pure, lovely fragrance of offerings consecrated by the Lord; who eats food offered to you and wears garments and ornaments as your grace; who bows the head upon seeing gods, guru, or brahmins and makes especially loving petitions to them. Such a person’s hands daily worship Rāma’s feet, and no second reliance occupies the heart. The feet walk to Rāma’s sacred places; the devotee continually recites your sovereign mantra and worships you together with your family. Such people offer libations and fire sacrifices by many prescribed rites, feed brahmins, and give abundant gifts. Knowing the guru inwardly to be greater even than you, they serve and honor the teacher in every way—Rāma, live within their minds.

Live, Raghurāya, in the hearts of those untouched by lust, anger, intoxication, pride, delusion, greed, agitation, attachment, or hatred, and free of deceit, pretension, and illusion. They are dear to all and work for everyone’s welfare; pain and pleasure, praise and abuse are alike to them. After reflection they speak words both truthful and kind, and awake or asleep they remain in your refuge. They know no other destination after leaving you; dwell in their minds, Rāma. They regard another’s wife as a mother and another’s wealth as poison more deadly than poison. They rejoice to see another’s prosperity and grieve especially at another’s misfortune. For those to whom you, Rāma, are dearer than life, their minds are auspicious homes for you. Live there with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, for you are their master, friend, father, mother, guru—everything.

Live in the pure minds of those who relinquish everyone’s faults and gather their virtues, and who endure hardship for the welfare of brahmins and cows. Those whose conduct is famed in the world for discernment of right policy have minds fit to be your home. One who understands your virtues and one’s own faults and trusts you in every way; one to whom Rāma’s devotees are dear—live in that heart with Vaidehī. One who abandons caste, lineage, wealth, religious status, prestige, beloved family, home, and comforts and keeps only you pressed to the heart—remain in that heart, Raghurāya. Heaven, hell, and liberation are equal to one who sees you everywhere holding bow and arrows. One who is your servant in deed, word, and thought is your dwelling. The mind of one who never asks anything from you and bears a natural love for you is your own perpetual home.

Having thus shown Rāma his inward dwellings, the eminent sage delighted him with loving words. He then named a timely, pleasant hermitage: “Live at Mount Citrakūṭa, scion of the Sun, where you will have every convenience. The mountain is lovely and the forest charming, the roaming ground of elephants, lions, deer, and birds. There is the holy river praised in the Purāṇas, brought forth through the ascetic power of Atri’s wife; its celestial-current stream is named Mandākinī and destroys the whole brood of sins. Many great sages, beginning with Atri, live there and discipline their bodies in yoga, recitation, and austerity. Go and bring everyone’s labor to fulfillment; by dwelling there, Rāma, bestow distinction upon the noble mountain.” The great sage sang Citrakūṭa’s boundless glory. Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa arrived and bathed in the excellent river.

entries.meaning: Rāma told Lakṣmaṇa that the landing place was good and asked him to establish a dwelling somewhere nearby. Lakṣmaṇa saw a firm bank descending to the water and examined the four directions. In the verse’s martial allegory the river is a bow, the five disciplines—including inner calm, self-restraint, and giving—are arrows, the sins of the Kali age are varied quarry, and steadfast Citrakūṭa is a hunter who never misses a close-struck target. Lakṣmaṇa then showed the selected place, and Rāma was pleased with the ground. The gods learned where Rāma’s heart had settled; Viśvakarmā came with the chief gods, all disguised as Kol and Kirāta forest people, and they fashioned beautiful homes of leaves and grass. The loveliness of the two huts cannot be described: one was graceful and small, the other spacious. Within this charming dwelling the Lord shone with Lakṣmaṇa and Jānakī, like Love in an ascetic’s dress accompanied by Rati and Spring.

alternatives: as the cord of a bow

entries.meaning: Gods, Nāgas, Kinnaras, and guardians of the directions came to Citrakūṭa at that time. Rāma bowed to everyone, while the delighted gods gained the reward of sight. Showering flowers, their assembly said, “Lord, today we who lacked a protector have found one.” After petitioning him and recounting their unbearable distress, they joyfully returned to their several homes. News spread that Raghunandana had made Citrakūṭa his shelter, and sages arrived as they heard it. Seeing the joyful company approach, the moon of Raghu’s line prostrated himself. The sages embraced Rāma and blessed him that his purposes might succeed; beholding the beauty of Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and Rāma, they counted every spiritual practice fulfilled. The Lord honored each appropriately and dismissed the sages, who freely resumed yoga, recitation, vigils, and austerity in their hermitages.

When the Kol and Kirāta forest communities received the news, they rejoiced as though the nine treasures had entered their homes. Filling leaf bowls again and again with tubers, roots, and fruit, they set out like paupers going to plunder gold. Those among them who had seen the two brothers answered the others’ questions along the road; talking and listening about Raghu’s hero’s beauty, all arrived and saw Raghurāya. They made respectful salutation, laid their gifts before him, and gazed on the Lord with intense love. They stood everywhere like painted figures, bodies thrilled and eyes overflowing with tears. Rāma knew them all to be immersed in love and honored each with affectionate words. Bowing to him repeatedly, they joined their hands and humbly said: “Now, Lord, we have all found a protector by seeing your feet. Our good fortune is your arrival, king of Kosala.”
